title: What tools did you make for game dev?
author: TheScriptan
selftext:
I am interested to see how others are creating internal tools for themselves to automate the process of game dev, either asset generation pipelines, performance optimization tools, rendering, or anything else?

  
I wanted to share mine:

![img](hkh62sg1chwh1 "AutoLOD for 3D models")

First one is auto-lod tool that creates three level of details assets from the original reducing vertices and triangles, thus improving the performance significantly for low-end devices!

I am working on an RTS and I want to squeeze out as much performance as I can from everything!

https://i.redd.it/bio359i8chwh1.png

Second is a wrapper over ADB to connect devices wirelessly automatically to save up manual work. I hate connecting Android devices, both wired and wireless, so I made a tool + custom APK where it auto-connects always under my home network. All of this is needed since I let my AI agents do performance tests, validate the changes or fine-tune pathfinding algorithms to make everything work fast.

So I am interested to see how other's are using AI to help them do game dev:)

  
If you're interested for more, you can follow me on X :D 

  
[https://x.com/Lizzergas](https://x.com/Lizzergas)

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: I made an asset builder where I was able to make most of my assets, that’s most of where I spent the first 3 months on my project and I still add to it. Levels, characters, items, and props, animations / cut scenes are all made in the asset builder. Audio is assigned there. Ect. It’s mostly layer and shape based as opposed to say free draw or pixel art. You can make test world seeds in the asset builder as well and give yourself weapons and items for testing (I’m not at my pc for screenshots / videos of it but I have around 400 assets made there, mostly props for levels but I’m at around 128/500 desired character items made in the asset maker

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
I made a couple of AI coding skills specifically for game development. The Unity one teaches the agent the architecture and performance rules I want it to follow: separate gameplay data from GameObjects, keep logic deterministic, prefer arrays for hot runtime data, avoid unnecessary allocations/GC, use pooling, validate data at tool time, and only reach for Burst/Jobs/ECS when profiling shows a reason.

What I like about this approach is that it moves a lot of the “code review” earlier. Instead of letting the AI generate whatever architecture it wants and cleaning it up afterward, the skill gives it the rules before it starts and can also review existing code for violations.

Unity version:  
[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/unity-data-oriented-design-skills](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/unity-data-oriented-design-skills)

Language-agnostic version:  
[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

The ideas behind both come from the architecture I use in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data-Oriented Design*:  
[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)

comments.author: Illustrious-Pay6341
comments.body:
Remember Game Maker by Mark Overmars? I started making games using GM 5 when I was 13 years old. It was one of the most intuitive software I have ever used and simplified the game making process so much that even my 13 year old brain could understand and make games. Once GM was bought by YoYo games and Mark left, I stopped using that tool and taught myself programming in C++ and went to university to get Comp Sci degree. So that software started my whole career as software engineer.

With the help of Claude, I wrote an entire game engine that looked and worked exactly like GM 5 but with new added features that allows you to create 3d games. I think the object->event->action concept is really intuitive and I could have just gone and used unreal engine or something but I wanted that nostalgic feeling I had when I was 13. It also has MCP server so when I am stuck, I can ask Claude to come by and help me.

For 3d asset, Claude set me up with an artifact page where I can draw sketches and upload them and Claude would then use that sketch to create 3d model. I can also describe the animation the model needs and Claude does that too. :)

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I wrote something for making consistent artwork, uses Gemini's api to make it pretty cheap for generations from text. I added the ability to add one or more reference photos, so you can refine your idea, and every prompt gets your custom style guidelines included. It now does image to 3d too, though I'm still tweaking that to try to get nice game-ready models. Did some of my own updates to Trellis2 to keep system memory usage a bit lower.

I have too many projects. So I made a project to manage my projects across multiple computers (unsaved work was spread everywhere.) Now I can see at a glance how many of my projects are sitting there waiting for me, where they're at, and ensuring I don't lose changes on a computer I'd forgotten about. 

I have too many assets I've acquired from Hunble Bundles and asset stores. I had to write something that would pull in all my purchases and catalogue them. Unity's in-editor asset browser doesn't even show pictures. And the assets are spread out across so many stores its easy to forget where/how I get to it later on. 

I'm enhancing these as new use cases and needs come to me. The last two I could probably open source, the Trellis2 changes already are.

I'm sure I'll make more as I think of them.
